question: Do frontier agents that can execute end-to-end LLM post-training also revise their high-level training strategy when experimental evidence says the initial strategy is failing, and can added experience, human guidance, or inference compute repair any deficit?

key_findings.claim: Current agents execute post-training pipelines competently but almost never change the training paradigm, data-source type, or stage structure after training begins.
key_findings.evidence: Across 1,338 released PostTrainBench trajectories, agents ran 5,111 verified trainings and improved average benchmark score from 10.41% to 23.0%. Yet only 74 of 3,557 recognized adjacent experiment pairs changed strategy, a 2.08% rate; 35 changed objective family, 38 data-source type, and one stage structure.

key_findings.claim: The initial strategy follows the agent or scaffold more strongly than the benchmark, indicating default-policy lock-in rather than task-conditioned strategic choice.
key_findings.evidence: Among recognized initial strategies, Claude Code chose full-parameter SFT in 163 of 202 cases (80.7%), while Codex CLI chose parameter-efficient fine-tuning in 268 of 299 cases (89.6%); the same direction held in all 28 matched benchmark-by-base-model cells.

key_findings.claim: Persistent experiment history, practical skills, and evaluator feedback substantially improve execution but do not cause strategic revision.
key_findings.evidence: With Qwen3-1.7B-Base and three runs per condition, the experience-driven Opus 4.6 scaffold scored 77.30% on GSM8K and 62.80% on HumanEval versus 64.70% and 22.00% for autonomous Opus 4.6. Nevertheless, the main agent adopted all logged execution-level suggestions and none of the strategy-level suggestions, including repeated proposals to switch HumanEval from SFT to RL or add an AIME SFT warm-up.

key_findings.claim: A human can redirect the plan before training, but the autonomous run subsequently collapses into local adjustment; more inference compute has the same execution-only ceiling on the hardest task.
key_findings.evidence: The human-guided AIME run reached 13.33% pass@8 and visibly changed the initial strategy, but later runs repeatedly tuned within that strategy after an early peak. The experience-driven scaffold used 7.9 times the baseline tokens on AIME, about 66.7 million tokens for one additional solved problem in its best run, a difference the authors treat as within the benchmark's variance.

key_findings.claim: The observed deficit is failure to initiate strategy reconsideration, not inability to understand or implement a different strategy.
key_findings.evidence: In the guided condition the agent understood a reviewer-proposed SFT-to-RL rationale, implemented it, and independently skipped an unnecessary SFT warm-up; in unguided conditions it sometimes recorded the alternative and even wrote its code without executing it.

method.core_idea: Separate execution-level iteration inside a fixed post-training strategy from strategy-level revision, then audit full agent trajectories and intervene on the three most plausible causes of strategy lock-in.
method.mechanism: The authors reconstruct commands, tool calls, edits, training jobs, evaluations, and checkpoints from PostTrainBench. A verified training requires an executed parameter update. Adjacent trainings are labeled as strategy changes only if the objective family, data-source type, or stage structure changes. Controlled experiments add an append-only experiment journal, a post-training skill library, and a separate evaluator; then add a binding human plan review; and finally treat the resulting two-to-eightfold token increase as a compute-scaled condition.
assumptions: The coarse three-component strategy state captures the consequential high-level revisions of interest.
LLM annotation followed by author review identifies executed strategies reliably despite incomplete data provenance.
PostTrainBench's ten-hour bounded-compute setting is representative enough to diagnose automated AI R&D behavior.
Rare switching is evidence of missing strategic comparison, not evidence that switching itself would usually improve results.
AIME's 30 problems make small score changes too noisy to interpret without trajectory evidence.

techniques.role: Distinguishes objective, data-source, and stage changes from hyperparameter tuning, debugging, reward shaping, and other within-strategy work.
Uses executed commands and artifacts rather than final scores alone to identify what agents actually tried.
Keeps plans, observations, evaluations, and lessons accessible across a long run.
Compresses checkpoint outputs and pipeline evidence into concrete diagnoses and possible strategy changes.
Forces a human-requested strategy revision before execution so starting-strategy quality can be separated from in-run revision.
Tracks whether later runs branch strategically, continue locally, or revert to earlier checkpoints.

evaluations.setting: 1,338 public PostTrainBench trajectories across seven benchmarks, four base models, 20 agent configurations, and ten hours on one H100 per trajectory.
evaluations.metric: Verified training count, final-checkpoint rate, and average pass@1 gain where base and submitted scores are both available.
evaluations.result: 5,111 trainings, 1,104 valid final checkpoints, and average score 10.41% to 23.0%.
evaluations.baseline: Each trajectory's original base model under the released benchmark protocol.

evaluations.setting: All adjacent training pairs with recognized strategy state in the released corpus.
evaluations.result: 74 of 3,557 pairs changed any strategy dimension (2.08%): 35 objective, 38 data source, one stage structure.
evaluations.baseline: 3,483 pairs that stayed within the current strategy.

evaluations.setting: Qwen3-1.7B-Base on GSM8K, HumanEval, and AIME 2025; three ten-hour runs on four A800 GPUs per condition.
evaluations.metric: Mean pass@1 for GSM8K and HumanEval; AIME score under the paper's controlled protocol.

evaluations.setting: AIME 2025 controlled intervention with a binding human review before autonomous execution.
evaluations.metric: Final checkpoint pass@8 plus trajectory-level strategy redirection.
evaluations.result: Best guided run reached 13.33% pass@8 and executed a revised RL-oriented plan, but peaked early and then remained in local adjustment loops.
evaluations.baseline: Autonomous and experience-driven runs under the same base model and evaluation; the paper warns the numeric score difference is within AIME variance.

evaluations.setting: Token-use comparison between autonomous and experience-driven agents on the three controlled tasks.
evaluations.result: The scaffold used roughly two to eight times more tokens; on AIME it used 7.9 times more and about 66.7M tokens per one extra solved problem in the best run.
evaluations.baseline: Autonomous agent token use and final checkpoint performance.

limitations: Author-stated: the released corpus is observational; model, scaffold, prompt, interface, and benchmark effects are entangled.
Author-stated: incomplete data provenance makes data-source changes lower-bound observations, and missing labels are not imputed.
Author-stated: low change rates do not prove that switching is usually optimal; audited switches include both gains and regressions.
Author-stated: AIME 2025 has only 30 problems, so one-problem changes are within substantial evaluation variance.
Reviewer inference: the controlled interventions use one small base model, three tasks, one principal scaffold, and three runs, limiting claims about larger models and other research domains.
Reviewer inference: the strategy taxonomy may classify consequential data-mixture or reward-design changes as execution even when they function strategically in practice.
failure_modes: An agent can respond to a plateau by repeatedly tuning learning rate, formatting, or data mixture while never testing the alternative objective its own evaluator recommends.
A long, tool-heavy context can overweight recent logs and local errors, crowding out reconsideration of the global plan.
A good human-approved initial plan can still degrade when new evidence arrives after the only mandatory review point.
Extra inference compute can densify search inside a bad strategy and therefore increase cost without reopening the high-level choice.
A strategy-change detector can miss revisions when data provenance or stage lineage is not identifiable in the execution trace.
reusable_insights: Treat strategy revision as an explicit action with decision points, evidence thresholds, and reward, rather than an optional sentence in a long context.
Evaluate research agents on trajectory structure and counterfactual testing, not only final benchmark gain.
Separate persistent evidence storage from the policy that decides when evidence invalidates a committed plan; memory alone does not create reconsideration.
Use binding review gates after meaningful regressions or plateaus, not only before the first experiment.
Track objective-family, data-source, and stage transitions as first-class telemetry for autonomous experimentation systems.
open_questions: Which training objective can reward warranted strategy reopening without encouraging wasteful switching?
Can a learned change-point or value-of-information trigger decide when a strategy comparison is worth its compute cost?
Does strategy lock-in persist for larger base models, larger agent models, longer budgets, and pre-training or architecture research?
Would periodic adversarial review, parallel strategy branches, or independent portfolio agents close the strategy loop more reliably than a single evaluator?
How should a benchmark score strategic judgment when the best alternative is expensive to test and its counterfactual outcome is unobserved?

competitive_landscape.title: PostTrainBench: Can LLM Agents Automate LLM Post-Training?
competitive_landscape.difference: PostTrainBench introduces the bounded-compute benchmark and reports final capability and safety failures; this paper re-analyzes its full trajectories to isolate execution from strategic revision and adds controlled causal interventions.

competitive_landscape.title: LLMZero: Discovering Adaptive Training Strategies for RL Post-Training via LLM Agents
competitive_landscape.difference: LLMZero uses tree search to discover multi-stage, checkpoint-conditioned RL schedules and reports gains over grid and random search; this paper does not propose a search system and instead shows why ordinary agents rarely initiate a branch away from their chosen strategy.

competitive_landscape.title: AutoLLMResearch: Training Research Agents for Automating LLM Experiment Configuration -- Learning from Cheap, Optimizing Expensive
competitive_landscape.difference: AutoLLMResearch trains configuration agents in a multi-fidelity environment to extrapolate from cheap to expensive experiments; this paper tests untrained frontier-agent workflows and identifies failure to reopen the objective, data, or stage choice even when evidence is available.

competitive_landscape.title: Agent^2 RL-Bench: Can LLM Agents Engineer Agentic RL Post-Training?
competitive_landscape.difference: Agent^2 RL-Bench evaluates whether agents can build increasingly interactive RL pipelines and diagnoses driver-dependent outcomes; this paper studies a broader seven-benchmark corpus and makes strategy persistence itself the measured failure.

novelty_assessment: Reviewer inference: the principal novelty is not another automated post-training scaffold but a trajectory-level capability decomposition, supported by a large observational audit and escalating interventions that distinguish missing memory, guidance, or compute from missing self-initiated strategy revision. PostTrainBench and Agent^2 RL-Bench establish that agents can run pipelines, while LLMZero and AutoLLMResearch add explicit search or trained research policies; this paper uniquely argues that the unaided frontier-agent loop is locally iterative but globally linear. The causal strength is limited because the lock-in corpus is observational and the controlled study is small.
reviewer_notes: Full main text and relevant appendices were read. Counts were checked against pages 3-4 and 16-18; controlled scores and token claims were checked against pages 5-9. Competitive metadata and abstracts were verified on primary arXiv pages. The interpretation that strategy taxonomy may undercount meaningful revisions is reviewer inference.
